propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of an immigration officer's decision dated August 10, 2016, refusing the Applicant's permanent residence application.
The refusal was based on failure to meet IRP Regulations requirements due to no qualifying offer of permanent employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of an immigration officer's refusal of the Applicant's permanent residence application for lack of qualifying employment.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is an Indian citizen who studied in Canada and worked at Horizon Travel Magazine starting October 2014 under a post-graduate work permit.
His work permit was renewed to July 2016 and Horizon applied for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) on his behalf, approved October 27, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is an Indian citizen who worked at Horizon with a renewed work permit and had an LMIA approved for him.

propositions.text: The Applicant submitted an Express Entry profile in September 2015 indicating a qualifying offer of arranged employment.
He received an invitation to apply for permanent residency on November 27, 2015, with 971 points including 600 for arranged employment.
He applied on January 22, 2016, including LMIA confirmation, but application was returned incomplete for missing medical and education documents.
He resubmitted, received a second invitation on February 10, 2016, and included LMIA approval and a January 18, 2015 letter from Horizon confirming employment.
He finalized submission in February 2016; application was refused on August 10, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Applicant's Express Entry submissions, invitations, incomplete and complete applications, and final refusal.

propositions.text: The Officer's refusal letter cited s 11.2 IRPA that a visa cannot be issued if applicant lacks qualifications on which they were ranked.
The Officer noted the Applicant indicated a qualifying offer in his profile but was not satisfied he had a permanent employment offer.
The Officer referenced Ministerial Instructions and s 82(2)(c) IRP Regulations regarding qualifying offers.
The Officer found the Applicant did not have a qualifying offer of arranged employment and refused the application accordingly.
The loss of qualification caused a points drop below the lowest ranking person invited under Express Entry CRS.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Officer's refusal based on lack of qualifying employment offer and resulting points drop below threshold.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes form part of the decision reasons, citing prior cases supporting their use.
Notes state Applicant awarded CRS points for qualifying job offer based on positive LMIA but did not submit an offer of employment.
The January 18, 2015 letter confirmed employment start, position, salary but lacked duties; Officer not satisfied of qualifying offer.
This resulted in a points drop below minimum CRS score for the round, leading to refusal under R82(1) and A11.2.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes GCMS records show Officer found no qualifying job offer despite LMIA and letter, causing points drop and refusal.

propositions.text: The Applicant raises two issues: breach of procedural fairness and reasonableness of the Officer's decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's two issues: procedural fairness breach and decision reasonableness.

propositions.text: Whether a visa officer erred by not raising concerns with applicant is a procedural fairness question reviewed on correctness standard.
Dunsmuir and other cases establish procedural fairness review standard as correctness for such issues.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness questions about officer's duty to raise concerns are reviewed on correctness standard per Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: The standard of review for officer's assessment of permanent residence applications is reasonableness.
Cites cases supporting reasonableness standard and high deference to officer's evidence assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness is the standard for reviewing officer's assessment of permanent residence applications, with high deference.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensibility of decision within facts and law.
Dunsmuir para 47 defines reasonableness standard.
Summarizes statutory framework of IRPA ss 10.3(1) and 11.2 regarding Ministerial Instructions and visa issuance criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness standard and summarizes IRPA provisions on Ministerial Instructions and visa issuance criteria.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter was sufficient evidence of qualifying permanent offer of arranged employment.
Duty of fairness requires officers to ask questions when concerns about credibility or genuineness arise.
Concerns about existence or genuineness of offer or ability to perform employment should have been put to Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues LMIA letter sufficed as evidence and officer should have raised concerns about genuineness or ability to perform job.

propositions.text: Officer has no duty to assist applicant absent credibility or authenticity concerns.
No duty to advise applicant of concerns from insufficient evidence submission.
Officer was not questioning credibility but was not satisfied Applicant had qualifying offer.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues no duty to assist or advise absent credibility concerns; Officer was not satisfied with qualifying offer.

propositions.text: The matter is sufficiency of evidence and reasonableness of Officer's conclusion on qualifying offer.
The court does not believe the Officer's finding was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the issue is evidence sufficiency and concludes the Officer's finding was reasonable.

propositions.text: No obligation on visa officer to provide opportunity to address concerns when documents are incomplete or insufficient.
Cites Pathirannahelage, Hamza, Gharialia, Veryamani, Rezvani supporting no duty to assist with incomplete evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers have no duty to offer opportunity to address concerns when evidence is incomplete or insufficient, citing cases.

propositions.text: Visa officers are not obligated to convey concerns arising from IRP Regulations or sufficiency of evidence.
Cites Gedara and Virk cases where officers had no duty to seek missing evidence or advise on sufficiency.
In Virk, officer reasonably required evidence of English proficiency and no breach of fairness found.

paragraphs.summary: The court states officers need not convey concerns about evidence sufficiency, citing Gedara and Virk where no duty to seek missing evidence existed.

propositions.text: No record suggests Officer doubted genuineness of application or documents.
Distinguishes disregarding evidence for genuineness doubts from finding evidence insufficient on balance of probabilities.
Officer found documents insufficient to prove qualifying offer for indeterminate period.
Officer reviewed January 18, 2015 letter and found it insufficient.
No duty to advise Applicant of concerns about insufficiency of evidence submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no genuineness concerns, distinguishes insufficiency from credibility, and finds no duty to advise on insufficient evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant claims procedural unfairness because application was refused, not returned incomplete, contrary to legitimate expectations.
Applicant expected incomplete applications to be returned based on FSW Manual and IRP Regulations ss 10(1)(c) and 12.
Applicant's initial application was returned incomplete for missing medical and education documents.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues refusal rather than return of incomplete application breached legitimate expectations based on prior practice and regulations.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks substantive right via legitimate expectations, but doctrine only confers procedural rights.
Passing initial completeness check does not shield applicant from failing regulatory requirements at second stage.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues legitimate expectations doctrine grants only procedural rights and does not prevent refusal for regulatory failures.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted documents for all required categories, so application was 'complete' in that sense.
Officer found documents insufficient to establish qualifying offer of permanent employment.
This differs from prior incomplete return for missing categories; here evidence was insufficient, not missing.
Doctrine of legitimate expectations does not apply in these circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the application was complete but evidence insufficient, distinguishing prior incomplete return, and rejects legitimate expectations claim.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter is sufficient evidence of qualifying permanent offer of arranged employment.
LMIA validates offer of employment per IRP Regulations ss 82(2), 203, 315.2.
Approval letter lists employer, Applicant's name, position, and continuous full-time permanent employment.
Applicant agrees LMIA is not determinative; officers can deny if concerns about ability or likelihood to perform job.
No such concerns were raised in this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues LMIA letter suffices as evidence of qualifying permanent employment and no concerns about ability to perform were raised.

propositions.text: No legislative basis requires an offer of employment; it is only a policy requirement, so failure to provide it cannot disqualify him
Having been awarded 971 points including 600 for arranged employment means the Officer accepted he had an offer of permanent employment
His LMIA post-dated his invitation and was valid when points were awarded, so providing an offer of employment was backwards looking
January 18, 2015 letter of employment proves he had employment; LMIA proves he had an offer of permanent employment which Officer failed to appreciate

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no legislative basis requires an offer of employment; points awarded show Officer accepted offer; LMIA post-dated invitation; January 18 letter proves employment, LMIA proves offer.

propositions.text: Visa officers are not bound by LMIA checks from Employment and Social Development Canada
Applicant was advised to include a job offer signed by him and employer in Express Entry checklist
Such a job offer is not superfluous and it is reasonable for officer to look for a permanent position statement
January 18, 2015 letter did not contain information about permanent position

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says visa officers not bound by LMIA checks; Applicant was advised to include signed job offer; job offer is not superfluous; January 18 letter lacks permanent position info.

propositions.text: LMIA is not a rubber stamp for permanent residency but allows points to be assessed and invitation issued if sufficient
Express Entry checklist is policy-prescribed; letter of offer content is clearly described
Applicant failed to submit a document meeting the requirements

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues LMIA allows points assessment but is not automatic; checklist is policy; Applicant failed to submit required document.

propositions.text: Applicant was required to satisfy Officer that s 82 IRP Regulations criteria were met, meaning employer offered arranged employment
s 82 IRP Regulations defines arranged employment as continuous full-time work in Canada for at least one year after permanent resident visa issuance
Plain reading of s 82 requires submission of an offer of employment

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant had to satisfy s 82 IRP Regulations requiring arranged employment offer for continuous full-time work for at least one year.

propositions.text: LMIA approval letter states foreign worker needs LMIA letter and Annex A to apply for work permit or permanent resident visa before LMIA expiry
CIC requires employment contract or job offer letter signed by employer and foreign worker before issuing work permit or permanent resident visa
LMIA does not authorize entry, stay or work; it is only one CIC requirement to issue permit or visa

paragraphs.summary: Court notes LMIA letter requires signed employment contract or job offer before permit or visa issuance; LMIA alone does not authorize entry or work.

propositions.text: Express Entry completeness check produces personalized document checklist identifying required supporting documents
Letter of offer confirms qualifying arranged employment and screens for fraud
Letter required only if applicant claims qualifying arranged employment

Letter must be on company letterhead and include specified details: start date, continuous full-time work for at least one year after visa issuance, job title, duties, current status, hours, salary, benefits
If LMIA associated, LMIA number requested but scanned LMIA not required at application submission

paragraphs.summary: Court describes Express Entry checklist requires letter of offer with detailed info to confirm arranged employment; LMIA number requested if applicable.

propositions.text: Applicant provided LMIA approval letter as offer and January 18, 2015 letter as letter of employment
Officer noted valid LMIA and considered January 18 letter but was not satisfied Applicant had qualifying offer confirming permanent position
January 18 letter confirms employment since October 2014 as web developer with salary but does not show forward-looking offer signed by both parties

paragraphs.summary: Applicant provided LMIA and January 18 letter; Officer noted LMIA but found January 18 letter did not show qualifying forward-looking offer signed by both.

propositions.text: Applicant's affidavit includes June 19, 2015 offer letter from Horizon offering permanent full-time web developer position signed by both parties
June 19 letter was not provided with permanent residence application and was not before Officer when decision made
Evidentiary record on judicial review is restricted to evidence before decision-maker; new evidence generally inadmissible
Limited exceptions to evidence rule exist but do not apply here (Assn of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency)
June 19, 2015 letter is not admissible evidence

paragraphs.summary: Court finds June 19, 2015 letter not before Officer and inadmissible on judicial review; evidence limited to record before decision-maker.

propositions.text: Decision-maker presumed to have considered all evidence before him or her (Kotanyan v Canada)
Officer notes in GCMS Notes that Applicant had valid LMIA with Horizon
LMIA approval letter was not an offer of employment

paragraphs.summary: Court presumes Officer considered all evidence; Officer noted valid LMIA; LMIA letter not an offer of employment.

propositions.text: No legislative basis absence; Officer relied on s 82 IRP Regulations and s 11.2 IRPA in refusal, not only policy
s 82 IRP Regulations requires employer offer of arranged employment defined as continuous full-time work for at least one year after visa issuance
Reasonable for Officer to require letter of offer to be satisfied of arranged employment
No undue reliance on non-binding policy; refusal under s 11.2 arose from IRP Regulations requirements

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably required offer letter under s 82 IRP Regulations; refusal based on law not just policy.

propositions.text: Court has accepted failure to submit documents requested under checklist may justify denial (Khan, Singh, Senadheera)
LMIA letter, checklist, and instructions informed Applicant of required document to satisfy arranged employment under s 82
LMIA post-dating invitation is irrelevant; letter required to confirm qualifying arranged employment and program requirements
Because letter not provided, Officer found Applicant lacked qualifications basis for points and invitation
Permanent residence denied under s 11.2 IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Court finds failure to submit required letter justified denial; LMIA post-date irrelevant; permanent residence denied under s 11.2 IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer could reasonably request offer meeting criteria; duty of fairness did not compel Officer to do so
Given documents provided, Officer reasonably found no qualifying job offer; decision within acceptable range

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably found no qualifying offer; duty of fairness did not require request; decision defensible.

propositions.text: Can officer revoke 600 points for arranged employment without legal reliance on subsection 29(2) MI and without opportunity to respond when LMIA valid but no letter of offer?
Can officer justify revoking 600 points based only on policy (FSW manual) absent legal authority and without opportunity to respond?
Can officer use other evidence filed by Applicant to find insufficiency without notice or opportunity to respond, triggering duty of fairness?
If Applicant claims 600 points for arranged employment, invited to apply, submits complete application, can officer refuse for no arranged employment even if 67 points scored on FSW grid?

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits four certification questions about officer's authority to revoke points, reliance on policy, use of evidence, and refusal despite points scored.

propositions.text: Test for certifying question: dispositive of appeal, transcend immediate parties, and involve broad significance (Zhang)
Question must have been raised and dealt with by Federal Court judge (Zhang)

paragraphs.summary: Court states certification test requires question to be dispositive, transcend parties, involve broad significance, and be dealt with by judge.

propositions.text: None of proposed questions meet certification test; no broad significance or transcendence; not dispositive given findings

paragraphs.summary: Court finds none of Applicant's questions meet certification test; no broad significance or dispositive effect.
